newsitem.title: UK: Nationalist violence flares after N.Ireland march.
newsitem.headline: Nationalist violence flares after N.Ireland march.

text.p: Angry Irish nationalists took to the streets of Northern Ireland in a wave of violence, firing on police and setting cars ablaze in protest at the holding of a Protestant Orange Order march in Portadown.

Police reported a series of shooting incidents across Belfast and elsewhere in the province, including an IRA attack on a patrol in the town of Coalisland in which a police woman received facial injuries.

Nationalist reaction erupted after police and army saturated Portadown to allow the pro-British Orange order to march on Sunday along its Garvaghy Road in the face of bitter opposition from Catholic residents.
Martin McGuinness, a senior figure in Sinn Fein, the IRA's political arm, called on Catholic nationalists to "take to the streets" in protest at the Garvaghy Road march.
Speaking in predominantly pro-Irish nationalist Londonderry, he said Catholics were like "the people of Chile, Nicaragua, El Salvador and South Africa.
"The place to be demanding justice is on the streets confronting your opponents," he said to wild applause.
As night fell in the city, masked youths hurled petrol bombs and fought running battles with police, who responded by firing plastic bullets.
In Belfast, shots were fired at police in at least two districts and hijackers burned cars and other vehicles.

Crowds of young people hung around on street corners on the Falls Road in Catholic west Belfast watching a dozen or more cars burn. Unexplained volleys of automatic gunfire rang out as army surveillance helicopters clattered over the city.
As the Garvaghy Road march broke up, youths threw rocks and other missiles at police. A total of 27 people, including 12 police officers, were hurt.

In nearby Lurgan, masked men hijacked a train and set it on fire after ordering passengers off. Later a gang returned to torch it a second time, police said. The reaction to the Garvaghy Road parade dealt a severe blow to Northern Ireland peace efforts sponsored by the British and Irish government.

The government of Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern made clear it was "deeply disappointed" by the British government's decision to allow the Orangemen to stage their march through a Catholic area of Portadown.
Ahern's government, in power since June 26, said in a statement that it had "left the British government in no doubt about our serious concern" over the way the parade was handled.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair has enjoyed record approval ratings since he won the May 1 general election by a landslide.
But in Northern Ireland, with its potential for more violence as the Protestant marching season moves into full swing, he faces perhaps the sternest test of his young administration.
Tension is unlikely to abate much in the run-up to July 12, the anniversary of the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, a milestone Protestant victory over invading Catholic forces.
It comes at the high point of the "marching season", when pro-British marching fraternities hold more than 2,500 parades across Northern Ireland.
The Orangemen say the parades are simply a demonstration of their beliefs and an assertion of their right to walk the "Queen's Highway", but Catholics see the marches as offensively triumphalist.
An Orange Order spokesman rejected this view of the Garvaghy Road parade.
"There have been no scenes of triumphalism," he said. "This is not a victory for anyone."

The Portadown parade was held just weeks after Blair reopened contacts with Sinn Fein to try to persuade its Irish Republican Army (IRA) backers to end their 28-year war against British rule to get Sinn Fein invited to the peace talks.

It is barred from the negotiations because of IRA violence and the province's pro-British Unionist leaders say it cannot be admitted until it has proved its democratic credentials by agreeing to a phased surrender of its weapons.
